paragraphs: Interactive imitation learning lets a learner ask an expert which action to take in particular states. The aim is to become competitive with that expert while requesting few annotations. This paper studies the agnostic setting: the learner’s available policy class may be unable to represent the expert’s policy exactly, making perfect imitation an unsuitable starting assumption.

The authors introduce MFTPL-P, short for Mixed Follow the Perturbed Leader with Poisson perturbations. It is an oracle-efficient algorithm with finite-sample guarantees that apply to any policy class. Those guarantees depend on access to samples from an additional explorative distribution over states. The broader coverage of policy classes is a central theoretical advance over the previous state of the art described in the abstract.

The paper also proposes Bootstrap-DAgger as a more practical variant that removes the need for this additional sample access. Together, the contributions address both formal learning guarantees under an explicit sampling assumption and an algorithm intended for a less demanding data-access setting.
icml-2024-agnostic-interactive-imitation.tldr: The paper develops broadly applicable guarantees for interactive imitation learning and a practical variant that avoids extra exploratory samples.

paragraphs: Generalization theory asks how reliably a learning algorithm’s performance on observed data carries over to new data. Algorithmic stability provides one way to study this question, but its usual analysis assumes that losses have a fixed upper bound. This paper extends that analysis to a broader setting in which losses can be unbounded.

The replacement condition is that the losses have a subweibull diameter, a probabilistic restriction governing their variability. Unbounded losses therefore remain subject to a specified tail condition. The resulting framework includes previously studied subgaussian and subexponential diameter conditions as special cases, bringing several forms of stability analysis into a common treatment.

The authors also refine the stability argument to obtain generalization bounds that can improve on earlier results by a factor of the square root of the sample size. This is a possible improvement under their analysis, rather than a universal rate for every learning problem. Their main technical contribution is a collection of concentration inequalities for subweibull random variables, which may also be useful beyond stability-based generalization.
icml-2024-algorithmic-stability-unleashe.tldr: New stability bounds accommodate unbounded losses under subweibull conditions and can improve previous bounds by a square-root-of-sample-size factor.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical inference for two equilibrium models. Linear Fisher markets describe fair and efficient allocation of resources, while first-price pacing equilibrium describes budget management in first-price auctions. Although these models serve different purposes, both can be characterized through an Eisenberg-Gale convex optimization program, providing a shared mathematical starting point.

The authors develop several statistically valid bootstrap procedures for these models. The objective is to support inference about equilibria, adding a statistical treatment to the underlying optimization formulation. Their most difficult case is general first-price pacing equilibrium, whose bootstrap analysis becomes a problem involving constrained M-estimators. The abstract identifies this constrained estimation problem as comparatively unexplored.

For first-price pacing equilibria with particular structures, the authors construct a procedure using epi-convergence theory. That structural qualification matters when interpreting the scope of the contribution. Experiments using synthetic and semi-real data support the theoretical analysis. Overall, the work connects equilibrium optimization with valid bootstrap inference and develops tools for handling the constraints that make this connection challenging.
icml-2024-bootstrapping-fisher-market-eq.tldr: The paper develops statistically valid bootstrap inference for Fisher markets and structured first-price pacing equilibria.

paragraphs: Robotic representation learning must connect several kinds of information: short and long stretches of task progress, visual changes over time, and the language instruction associated with an entire trajectory. Existing approaches often assign separate objectives to these goals. DecisionNCE introduces a unified objective intended to learn these properties together.

The method starts from an implicit preference: an observed visual trajectory should align better with its corresponding instruction than with a mismatched instruction. By changing how rewards are represented, the authors turn the Bradley-Terry preference model into a representation-learning framework. The resulting objective resembles InfoNCE but is adapted to decision-making tasks.

Within this framework, implicit comparisons across time encourage temporal consistency, while joint visual and language encoding grounds trajectories in instructions. The representation also captures both local and global task progression. Evaluations with simulated and real robots show that DecisionNCE supports diverse downstream policy-learning tasks. These findings support the usefulness of combining representation and reward learning around trajectory-level preferences, rather than treating each desired property as an isolated training goal.
icml-2024-decisionnce-embodied-multimoda.tldr: DecisionNCE uses implicit trajectory–instruction preferences to jointly learn task progress, temporal consistency, and language grounding for robots.

paragraphs: Underwater salient instance segmentation identifies prominent individual objects and their pixel boundaries in underwater images. Complex underwater conditions and difficulty adapting models to this domain can reduce accuracy. The paper addresses both this modeling problem and a shortage of large datasets with the detailed instance annotations needed to train and evaluate such systems.

The authors introduce USIS10K, containing 10,632 underwater images with pixel-level annotations across seven categories and varied underwater scenes. They also develop USIS-SAM, an underwater-specific architecture based on the Segment Anything Model. Its Underwater Adaptive Visual Transformer encoder brings visual prompts tailored to underwater imagery into the segmentation network.

A second component, the Salient Feature Prompter Generator, automatically produces prompts for salient objects. This replaces the explicit foreground points or boxes otherwise supplied as SAM prompts in the described setup. Experiments on USIS10K report superior performance over state-of-the-art comparison methods. The contribution combines a dedicated evaluation resource with domain adaptation and automatic prompting, addressing complementary obstacles to underwater segmentation.
icml-2024-diving-into-underwater-segment.tldr: USIS-SAM adapts Segment Anything to underwater imagery with automatic prompts, alongside a new dataset of 10,632 annotated images.

paragraphs: Precision and recall provide useful measurements for evaluating generative models, but their computational demands can become impractical as image datasets grow. This paper proposes efficient precision and recall, or eP&R, to preserve almost the same evaluation results while substantially reducing the time and memory needed to compute them.

The authors identify redundant work in two parts of the original calculation: computing ratios and deciding whether samples fall inside or outside the relevant manifold. They address both through hubness-aware sampling. A sample’s hubness counts how often it appears among other samples’ nearest neighbors in feature space. These counts guide the selection of representative real and generated images.

The sampling method is relatively insensitive to exact nearest-neighbor results, allowing the authors to use approximate nearest-neighbor methods for further efficiency. Extensive experiments show close agreement with the original precision and recall measurements, alongside substantially lower time and space costs. The finding supports a practical way to scale an existing evaluation approach while maintaining its reported results closely.
icml-2024-efficient-precision-and-recall.tldr: Hubness-aware sampling makes generative-model precision and recall much cheaper to compute while producing nearly identical results.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an available dataset rather than continually collecting new experience. Limited data coverage makes value estimation difficult, particularly for states absent from the dataset. This paper addresses that problem by combining the usual discrete-time value-learning approach with information drawn from continuous-time reinforcement learning.

The method first uses a discrete-time algorithm to learn a value function from the data. It also constrains the function’s first derivative to agree with local state and action characteristics described by the continuous-time Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. This adds information about how values should change locally to the value relationships supplied by discrete-time Bellman updates.

The authors provide practical versions for both deterministic and stochastic policy-gradient methods. Experiments on D4RL show that adding this first-order information significantly improves offline policy performance. The contribution is therefore a way to enrich value-function training using local dynamics, with implementations spanning two policy-learning settings. The reported results support the usefulness of that additional structure when learning from a fixed dataset with limited coverage.
icml-2024-enhancing-value-function-estim.tldr: Combining discrete-time value learning with continuous-time derivative constraints improves offline reinforcement learning performance on D4RL.

paragraphs: Evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning offer different ways to search for effective policies. Many methods combine them, but it remains unclear which integration mechanisms work well together. This paper examines that design question systematically, aiming to identify combinations that support more effective policy optimization.

The analysis organizes existing mechanisms into five perspectives: how the two approaches interact, how individual policies are structured, which evolutionary algorithms and operators are used, how evolution affects reinforcement learning, and how fitness surrogates are constructed and applied. The authors evaluate individual mechanisms and use experiments to investigate why the more effective choices help.

They then assemble the most effective mechanisms into EvoRainbow and EvoRainbow-Exp. Across tasks with different characteristics, these methods outperform strong baselines and achieve the state-of-the-art performance reported in the abstract. The contribution includes both the resulting algorithms and an empirical examination of design choices. This makes the work relevant to understanding how evolutionary and reinforcement-learning components can be combined, as well as to obtaining stronger policy-search performance.
icml-2024-evorainbow-combining-improveme.tldr: EvoRainbow combines empirically effective evolutionary and reinforcement-learning mechanisms to improve policy search across varied tasks.

paragraphs: In contextual dueling bandits, a learner chooses two options using the current context and observes which option is preferred. The feedback is a comparison rather than a separate reward for each choice. This paper develops a posterior-sampling approach for the linear version of this problem, where earlier algorithms had used upper confidence bounds.

The proposed algorithm, FGTS.CDB, adapts Thompson sampling through a specially designed Feel-Good exploration term. Its construction uses independence between the two selected options to avoid a cross term in the mathematical analysis. This is the central mechanism supporting the paper’s theoretical treatment of exploration in the paired-choice setting.

The authors prove regret scaling of approximately d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where d is model dimension and T is the time horizon. They characterize this rate as nearly minimax optimal. Synthetic-data experiments also show FGTS.CDB outperforming existing algorithms by a large margin. The paper thus supplies both a near-optimal theoretical guarantee and empirical evidence within its synthetic evaluations.
icml-2024-feel-good-thompson-sampling-fo.tldr: FGTS.CDB brings Thompson sampling to linear contextual dueling bandits with nearly minimax-optimal regret and strong synthetic-data results.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations model changing systems, but conventional training can be computationally expensive and susceptible to local optima. Fourier NODEs addresses these challenges by training the neural network to match an estimated vector field directly. This turns estimates of how observations change into explicit learning targets.

Fourier analysis estimates temporal derivatives and, when relevant, higher-order spatial derivatives from noisy observations. The spatial estimates become additional network inputs, while the temporal derivative becomes the desired output. The trained network then generates additional points through an ODE solver that stays outside the computational graph. Those points support improved Fourier-based derivative estimates in the next stage.

The alternating steps form a feedback loop between estimating derivatives and fitting dynamics. The framework is described as simulation-free training even though an ODE solver generates additional data outside the training graph. Across representative complex systems, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in training time, dynamics prediction, and robustness. These results support the approach of matching estimated local dynamics while refining the data used to estimate them.
icml-2024-from-fourier-to-neural-odes-fl.tldr: Fourier NODEs alternates derivative estimation and direct vector-field fitting to improve the speed and accuracy of dynamics modeling.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers use attention and structural information to learn representations of graphs. This paper argues that existing approaches often overlook information arising from relationships between different graphs. Its motivating idea is that graphs with similar structures should receive similar representations, making inter-graph correlations useful information for representation learning.

The authors introduce Graph External Attention, or GEA, to capture these correlations implicitly. The mechanism uses multiple external key-value units for nodes and edges. These units provide a means of incorporating information beyond the structure and interactions considered within a single graph, addressing the external-information gap identified by the paper.

GEA becomes part of Graph External Attention Enhanced Transformer, or GEAET. The architecture combines local structural information with global interactions to produce more comprehensive graph representations. Extensive benchmark experiments show state-of-the-art empirical performance. The reported findings support the usefulness of incorporating inter-graph information alongside local and global graph features, with the performance claim grounded in the evaluated benchmark datasets.
icml-2024-graph-external-attention-enhan.tldr: GEAET improves graph representations by adding external attention that implicitly captures correlations between graphs.

paragraphs: An autoencoder compresses high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation, but preserving the meaningful relationships between data points requires choosing an appropriate geometry. This paper questions the common assumption that ordinary Euclidean geometry in the original data space captures those relationships. Semantic or domain-specific similarities may instead be expressed more accurately by a suitable graph.

Given a similarity graph over the data points, the authors derive geometry from its graph Laplacian. They use a Riemannian geometric distortion measure as a training regularizer, encouraging the latent representation to preserve that geometry. The framework also makes this regularization suitable for larger-scale autoencoder training.

Experiments show better preservation of graph geometry than existing state-of-the-art geometry-preserving and graph-based autoencoders. The method is particularly effective for learning dynamics in latent space. Its central premise is the availability of a well-designed similarity graph: that graph supplies the relationships the representation should retain. The results support using this supplied geometry to guide compression and subsequent learning of dynamics.
icml-2024-graph-geometry-preserving-auto.tldr: A graph-derived geometric regularizer helps autoencoders preserve meaningful latent structure and learn dynamics in latent space.

paragraphs: Codebooks support image representations that use discrete distributions in latent space. Their success in generation motivates this paper’s central question: what arrangement of codebook entries works better? The authors focus on the distribution of the codebook itself, seeking a compact and structured organization for learned image representations.

Inspired by Kepler’s conjecture, they formulate codebook training through a sphere-packing problem and derive the Kepler codebook distribution. Training incorporates that distribution as a regularization target and uses a codebook partition method. This translates a geometric organizing principle into a practical way to shape the learned codebook.

Experiments evaluate image reconstruction and generation using natural-image and human-face datasets, respectively, and report significant performance improvements. The trained codebook also shows superior performance across datasets and when reconstructing images at different resolutions. These findings suggest that the organization imposed during codebook training can benefit several uses of image representations, including transfer across the evaluated datasets and resolution settings. The contribution centers on improving representation structure through the codebook’s geometry.
icml-2024-kepler-codebook-b348b97331.tldr: Kepler codebooks use a sphere-packing-inspired distribution to improve image reconstruction, generation, and performance across datasets and resolutions.

paragraphs: Maximum likelihood fitting for latent-variable models can be reformulated as minimizing a free-energy functional over model parameters and probability distributions. Earlier work used this viewpoint together with optimal transport to construct particle-based fitting algorithms. This paper develops that line of work by introducing momentum through a dynamical-systems formulation.

The proposed continuous-time system combines elements of Nesterov acceleration, underdamped Langevin diffusion, and particle methods. The guiding idea comes from interpreting momentum-based optimization algorithms as discrete versions of differential equations. Here, that connection is extended to the larger optimization space involved in free-energy minimization for latent-variable models.

Under suitable assumptions, the authors prove that the continuous-time system minimizes the functional. They then discretize it to obtain a practical maximum likelihood algorithm. Numerical experiments show that this algorithm outperforms existing particle methods and compares favorably with other maximum likelihood approaches. The theory establishes the continuous-time result under its assumptions, while the experiments demonstrate the practical value of the resulting discrete algorithm in the evaluated problems.
icml-2024-momentum-particle-maximum-like.tldr: A momentum-based dynamical system yields a practical particle algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation with favorable numerical results.

paragraphs: This paper estimates how much text in a large collection may have been substantially generated or modified by a language model. Its maximum likelihood approach uses expert-written and AI-generated reference texts to analyze patterns across a corpus. The intended measurement concerns the collection as a whole, including signals that may be too subtle to detect in individual documents.

The authors apply the method to peer reviews from ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, and EMNLP 2023. Their results suggest that 6.5% to 16.9% of review text could have undergone substantial LLM modification. This refers to changes beyond spelling corrections or minor edits, and remains an estimate of possible substantial modification.

Higher estimated fractions occur in reviews with lower reported confidence, reviews submitted near deadlines, and reviews from people less likely to respond to rebuttals. These are observed associations with estimated LLM use. The findings motivate broader study of how language models affect peer review and knowledge practices, while showing the value of measuring changes at corpus scale.
icml-2024-monitoring-ai-modified-content.tldr: Corpus-level analysis suggests that 6.5%–16.9% of text in the studied conference reviews could have been substantially modified by LLMs.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks directions that capture the variation in a dataset. Deflation finds these directions sequentially, beginning with the most important component and continuing to less important ones. Because each stage depends on earlier estimates, numerical inaccuracies can carry forward and affect components computed later.

This paper mathematically characterizes that error propagation for inexact Hotelling’s deflation. One analysis treats the procedure for estimating the leading eigenvector as an abstract subroutine. This provides a framework that can represent multiple algorithms and describes how their imperfect estimates influence subsequent stages of the deflation process.

A second analysis specializes to power iteration. Using information about the directions of the errors produced by that method, the authors obtain a tighter bound than the algorithm-independent analysis permits. Both cases explicitly describe how inaccuracies progress through successive component estimates. The contribution clarifies the consequences of sequential approximation and shows why accounting for a particular subroutine’s error structure can sharpen the analysis of the overall PCA procedure.
icml-2024-on-the-error-propagation-of-in.tldr: The paper characterizes error propagation in sequential PCA and derives tighter bounds when deflation uses power iteration.

paragraphs: Understanding how the structure of metallic glasses determines their properties remains difficult. This paper studies energy barriers as an intermediate target for investigating that relationship. The authors contribute a new prediction dataset and SymGNN, a graph neural network designed to predict these barriers from representations of metallic-glass structures.

SymGNN aggregates over orthogonal transformations of the graph structure. This gives the model E(3) invariance in expectation, a qualified symmetry property rather than an assertion of exact invariance for every individual evaluation. In energy-barrier prediction, the authors report greater accuracy than molecular-dynamics local-sampling methods and other machine-learning models.

Compared with precise molecular-dynamics simulations, prediction on new metallic glasses falls from roughly 41 days to less than one second in the reported comparison. The authors also apply explanation algorithms to identify structures associated with energy barriers. Those structures agree with the medium-range-order hypothesis and have distinctive topological properties. The work therefore combines fast prediction with structural interpretation, providing evidence relevant to the relationship between material organization and energy barriers.
icml-2024-predicting-and-interpreting-en.tldr: SymGNN predicts metallic-glass energy barriers rapidly and identifies explanatory structures consistent with the medium-range-order hypothesis.

paragraphs: Unsupervised adaptation of CLIP becomes more complicated when unlabeled data include classes outside the known set. This paper studies that setting, aiming to improve both recognition of known classes and detection of out-of-distribution samples. The setup extends beyond approaches that rely on class-name knowledge associated with the data’s ground-truth labels.

Universal Entropy Optimization, or UEO, uses each sample’s confidence to guide its treatment. It approximately minimizes conditional entropy for confident instances and maximizes marginal entropy for less confident ones. The distinction matters: the second objective operates on marginal predictions, rather than simply imposing the same confidence objective on every image.

The method adapts both the textual prompt and channel-wise affine transformations in CLIP’s visual branch. Experiments span 15 domains and four types of prior knowledge, supporting its effectiveness relative to baseline methods. The findings show the value of confidence-dependent adaptation when unlabeled data mix known and unknown classes, with both recognition and out-of-distribution detection included in the learning objective.
icml-2024-realistic-unsupervised-clip-fi.tldr: UEO adapts CLIP using confidence-dependent entropy objectives to improve known-class recognition and unknown-class detection in unlabeled data.

paragraphs: A convolutional network’s receptive field determines the spatial region involved in processing visual information. Its size is an important architectural choice. This paper introduces Mixture of Receptive Fields, or MoRF, which combines several receptive-field sizes and treats them as experts available to the network.

The approach serves two purposes: selecting a receptive field suited to the input and increasing network capacity. The authors develop hard and soft routing mechanisms to choose among these experts automatically. At inference, selected experts are merged through re-parameterization, with the aim of retaining a speed similar to a network using a single receptive field.

The authors incorporate MoRF into architectures including ResNet and ConvNeXt. Experiments report improvements over their baselines in image classification, object detection, and segmentation, without significantly increasing inference time. These findings support the practical value of making receptive-field choice adaptable while controlling execution cost. The contribution combines a broader set of spatial processing options with a mechanism for using those options efficiently during inference.
icml-2024-receptive-fields-as-experts-in.tldr: MoRF routes inputs among receptive-field experts and merges selected experts for improved vision performance with little inference-time increase.

paragraphs: Recommendation data can be biased because observed user behavior does not represent the target population. Some correction methods fill in missing labels, but their validity depends heavily on those imputed labels being accurate. This paper develops estimators that tolerate particular forms of systematic imputation error while preserving an unbiasedness guarantee.

The proposed doubly robust estimators are unbiased under either of two conditions. One permits arbitrary user-specific bias, item-specific bias, or a combination of both in the imputed labels. The other requires accurate learned propensities. The relaxation concerns these specified forms of bias; it does not make unrestricted imputation errors harmless.

The authors also introduce propensity reconstruction learning, using attention to adaptively update constraint weights and control variance. Experiments on one semi-synthetic dataset and three real-world datasets show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a weaker imputation requirement with a practical training approach, addressing both the validity of bias correction and the variability that can complicate its use in collaborative filtering.
icml-2024-relaxing-the-accurate-imputati.tldr: New doubly robust estimators tolerate specified user- and item-dependent imputation biases or remain unbiased when learned propensities are accurate.

paragraphs: This paper builds a scalable clustering method around the expected structure of kernel matrices. Its theory assumes an unknown isotropic Gaussian data distribution. For a Gaussian kernel with sufficiently separated cluster means, the expected kernel matrix can be close to a rank-k matrix, where k is the number of clusters.

The authors also bound the normalized kernel matrix’s deviation from its expectation in Frobenius norm. The deviation scales approximately as the inverse square root of sample dimension, up to logarithmic factors. These results motivate fitting each base kernel with a rank-k matrix that serves as a proxy for its expectation, then combining the proxies into a consensus rank-k representation.

An anchor-based construction makes the framework flexible about input matrix sizes and suitable for large datasets. The authors provide two non-asymptotic approximation bounds covering the consensus kernel and clustering indicator matrices. Experiments examine both clustering performance and the proposed theory. The approach links its low-rank clustering design to explicit distributional and separation conditions rather than assuming such structure without justification.
icml-2024-scalable-multiple-kernel-clust.tldr: The method combines low-rank approximations of expected kernel structure into a scalable clustering framework supported by conditional theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving machine learning can execute models securely, but nonlinear computations remain particularly expensive. Reducing them can lower execution cost while harming accuracy. Seesaw addresses this tradeoff through neural architecture search tailored to private inference, looking for architectures that use costly nonlinear operations more economically.

Its key strategy is to compensate for fewer nonlinear operations with additional linear computation and reuse of nonlinear results. Specialized pruning and search procedures manage the enlarged design space containing both kinds of operators. The search also considers accuracy alongside online and offline execution latency, so its choices account for more than the time spent answering a query.

For ImageNet classification at 71% accuracy, Seesaw reports 1.68-fold lower online latency and 1.55-fold lower combined online and offline latency than the state-of-the-art comparison design. At an equal latency of 190 seconds, it instead reports 3.65% higher accuracy. The authors also report simpler, faster search and training. These comparisons demonstrate distinct operating points where reallocating computation improves the accuracy–latency tradeoff.
icml-2024-seesaw-compensating-for-nonlin.tldr: Seesaw improves private-inference tradeoffs by replacing some expensive nonlinear work with linear computation and reuse of nonlinear results.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often work well when neighboring nodes have similar labels or features. Heterophilic graphs present a different situation: connected nodes can be dissimilar. Signed message passing is widely used to adapt graph learning to this setting, but this paper examines shortcomings that had lacked sufficient theoretical and empirical analysis.

The authors identify two problems. Signed message passing can produce undesirable representation updates involving neighbors reached through multiple hops. It also remains vulnerable to oversmoothing, in which node representations become insufficiently distinct. These findings show why introducing signed interactions alone may leave important difficulties in learning from heterophilic graphs.

The proposed remedy is Multiset to Multiset GNN, or M2M-GNN, a new message-passing function. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments show that it alleviates the identified weaknesses and achieves superior comparative performance. The contribution therefore includes both a diagnosis of signed message passing and an alternative supported by theory and evaluation. Its stated result is mitigation of these problems, rather than their universal elimination.
icml-2024-sign-is-not-a-remedy-multiset-.tldr: M2M-GNN alleviates multi-hop update problems and oversmoothing identified in signed message passing for heterophilic graphs.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that perform across a set of environments, potentially including unknown test environments. This requires optimizing over multiple distributions, making learning harder than in a fixed environment. The paper addresses the additional challenge of learning robustly from a single sequence of experience without building an environment model.

The proposed distributionally robust Q-learning algorithm, DRQ, uses a multi-timescale framework to process incrementally arriving samples. It is designed to make full use of each sample and directly learn the optimal distributionally robust policy. This allows training along one trajectory in a fully model-free fashion, addressing restrictions in earlier approaches described by the authors.

The paper establishes asymptotic convergence by extending classical stochastic approximation tools to the algorithm’s structure. That guarantee concerns convergence in the limit. Experiments additionally show improved robustness and sample complexity compared with non-robust methods and other robust reinforcement-learning algorithms. Together, these contributions connect a demanding robust optimization objective with a learning procedure compatible with sequentially collected experience.
icml-2024-single-trajectory-distribution.tldr: DRQ learns distributionally robust policies from a single trajectory without modeling the environment and has asymptotic convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: State perturbations can undermine reinforcement-learning agents, and an optimal robust policy need not be straightforward to establish. This paper introduces a consistency assumption stating that optimal actions remain consistent under small perturbations. The authors support this assumption with theoretical and empirical evidence, then use it to establish a conditional existence result.

Under that assumption, they prove that a deterministic, stationary optimal robust policy exists and agrees with the Bellman optimal policy. They further show the necessity of using the infinity norm when minimizing Bellman error to attain the optimal robust policy in their analysis. This emphasizes control of the largest error and helps explain vulnerabilities in approaches using an L1 Bellman-error objective.

The resulting algorithm, Consistent Adversarial Robust Deep Q-Network, minimizes a surrogate of Bellman infinity-error. CAR-DQN achieves top-tier performance across the evaluated benchmarks. The paper therefore connects an explicit assumption about action consistency to both a robustness theorem and a practical training objective, with experiments supporting the usefulness of that objective.
icml-2024-towards-optimal-adversarial-ro.tldr: Under an action-consistency assumption, the paper establishes an optimal robust policy and motivates CAR-DQN’s Bellman infinity-error objective.
